strengths: Novel latent-space policy optimization paradigm elegantly addresses the dimensionality bottleneck that has limited prior RL-based registration methods to low-dimensional transforms, while preserving fine spatial granularity through operation in learned encoder features

Latent-Dimension Variance Normalization (LDVN) is a technically sound and well-motivated contribution showing that variance scaling as O(N) can be controlled to O(1) by setting s ∝ √N, with correct unbiasedness proof and practical validation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse 3D benchmarks (OASIS, LiTS, Abdomen MR-CT), three backbone architectures, with consistent Dice improvements (2-4%), significant NJD reductions, proper statistical testing, and thorough ablation studies

Strong label efficiency results demonstrating 98.5% of full-label performance with only 60% of labeled data (Figure 4), directly addressing a critical practical challenge in medical imaging where annotations are scarce

Practical computational efficiency with minimal parameter overhead (<3%), single-step inference latency nearly unchanged, and clear architectural modularity enabling generalization across different backbones

Well-organized presentation with clear motivation, informative figures, and ablations (Tables 2-3) that convincingly demonstrate synergistic effects of multi-trajectory GRPO, warm-up, and LDVN components
weaknesses: Theoretical justification for LDVN relies on poorly-defined 'weak dependence' assumption; O(N) scaling derivation assumes near-independence of log-likelihoods across spatial dimensions, but correlated features may violate this. Formal statement of assumptions needed or empirical validation of assumption violations required

Unfair SPAC baseline comparison: 8-point Dice gap (78.92% vs 87.16%) lacks tuning details, ablations, or justification for dramatic underperformance. No analysis of whether SPAC is properly configured or directly comparable; weakens RL-based registration claims

GRPO choice lacks justification; no comparison with PPO/TRPO variants or analysis of fixed-prior trust region vs. ratio-clipping trade-offs. Why is GRPO specifically better for high-dimensional latent-space policy learning beyond implementation convenience?

Insufficient analysis of learned latent space: no visualization of Gaussian distributions, semantic meaning of high-dimensional latent vectors, or how representations differ between warm-up and fine-tuning phases. This undermines understanding of why latent-space policy learning is effective

Multi-step inference incurs 3× latency (625→2022ms) with only guidance that accuracy-speed trade-off is 'acceptable.' No concrete guidance on when practitioners should use 1 vs. 3 steps, or accuracy-vs-latency curves comparing methods

Extensive hyperparameter space (λ_scale, σ_min, σ_max, τ, λ_reg, β_KL, λ_warm, λ_Dice, w_Dice, w_NJD) with limited sensitivity analysis beyond trajectory/step counts (Table 2). Temperature τ, scaling factor s computation, and loss weight selections not justified

Loss function design (Eq. 16) weighting choices (λ_warm, λ_Dice) appear ad-hoc; different weighting strategies not ablated. Justification for hard-label rewards vs. soft-label Dice loss is brief and insufficient

Data preprocessing and augmentation strategies inadequately detailed (e.g., how 414 OASIS volumes become 400 pretraining pairs); reproducibility concerns without full pipeline description. No cross-validation or confidence intervals on small test sets
No failure case analysis: Table 2 shows NJD degrades beyond 3 steps, but mechanism is not explained. When does step-wise refinement provide minimal benefit? Which patient cases are problematic?

Statistical testing issues: Wilcoxon tests across multiple tasks without Bonferroni correction; small test sets (19 OASIS, 40 LiTS, 8 Abdomen) limit statistical power. Confidence intervals more informative than p-values alone

strengths: Well-motivated latent-space policy optimization paradigm that makes RL tractable for high-dimensional dense deformation fields
Principled LDVN contribution with solid mathematical justification (variance analysis O(√N)) and empirical validation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three 3D benchmarks, three backbones, with proper statistical significance testing
Exceptional label efficiency: 98.5% of full performance with only 60% of training data vs. 80% for baseline
Thorough ablation studies clearly decomposing component contributions and revealing saturation behavior (Tables 2-3)
Strong empirical results with consistent improvements (2-4% Dice, 30-60% NJD reduction) across diverse registration tasks
Excellent reproducibility with extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, and dataset protocols in supplementary material
Architectural agnosticism adding <3% parameters across different backbones
Insightful analysis of failure modes (e.g., Section 9 explaining SPAC's NJD reporting issues)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (GRPO, multi-step refinement) in latent space with LDVN normalization borrowed from Transformer attention scaled dot-product
Warm-up design (deterministic τ=0) lacks theoretical justification for preventing posterior collapse; appears ad-hoc despite empirical validation
High hyperparameter sensitivity and brittleness: only 33% stable training without warm-up vs. 79% with it; exploration temperature τ shows extreme sensitivity (τ=1: 83% vs τ=15: 56% Dice)
Computational efficiency claims overstated: 7-10% single-step overhead plus linear multi-step scaling (3× for T=3) may be prohibitive for clinical deployment
Unfair baseline comparisons: different methods follow different training protocols; SPAC results exclude NJD metric; not all baselines trained in unified setting
Minimal failure analysis: only one visual failure case (reward hacking); no systematic characterization of when/why method fails across anatomical structures
Weak-dependence assumption (Eq. 23) empirically verified only on OASIS+TransMorph; generalization to other architectures and datasets unclear
Limited scope and generalization: only demonstrated on 3D medical imaging registration; claims about general dense prediction tasks unvalidated
Incomplete analysis of design choices: no justification for greedy best-trajectory selection (Eq. 16) vs. alternatives; limited ablation on loss weight combinations
Hyperparameter tuning burden: requires careful balancing of λ_warm, λ_Dice, τ scheduling, σ clipping—limiting practical applicability
